name: broker
context: Distributed systems requiring location transparency and decoupling of clients from servers through an intermediate mediator component. The broker provides name resolution, request routing, and protocol translation to enable communication between heterogeneous components across network boundaries.
benefits: Loose coupling: producers and consumers don't need direct network knowledge
Location transparency: services reference each other by name, not IP/port
Language interoperability: IDL bridges C++, Java, Python, and other languages
Scalability: consumers can scale independently via queue partitioning
Resilience: message buffering, retries, and durable queues provide fault tolerance
Extensibility: add new consumers without modifying producers
Dynamic service location: servers can change IP/port without client updates
tradeoffs: Broker becomes single point of failure if not replicated
Complex debugging and tracing due to indirection
Operational complexity of managing broker infrastructure
Potential bottleneck if broker is not properly scaled
use_cases: Heterogeneous systems across languages and platforms needing interoperability
Dynamic service locations where servers change IP/port frequently
Enterprise integration with many services requiring decoupling
Service discovery and name resolution in distributed systems
Task queues and background job processing
avoid_when: Simple local communication only without network boundaries
Ultra-low latency requirements (<1ms) where broker overhead is unacceptable
Direct network access is simple and adequate for the use case
Synchronous request-response is critical and latency must be minimal
Small system with minimal complexity that doesn't justify broker overhead
Strong consistency requirements within single process boundary
component_types: Broker (ORB Core): Central mediator managing name-resolution, request routing, and protocol translation. Provides location transparency so clients reference servers by name, not address
Naming Service: Maintains associations between object names and their current locations (like DNS or Windows Registry)
Message Router: Routes requests from clients to appropriate servers based on naming information
Client Proxy (Stub): Implements server interface locally, handles marshalling/serialization of requests, delegates to broker
Server Proxy (Skeleton): Receives demarshalled requests, dispatches to actual server implementation
Parameter Marshalling: Translates data structures between local language format and common format (IDL)
Bridge: Optional component connecting brokers across networks or with different protocols
Producer: Emits messages (commands, events, requests) to the broker
Consumer: Subscribes to messages from the broker and processes them
Dead Letter Queue (DLQ): Captures failed messages for later analysis and retry
anti_patterns: Distributed monolith: using broker but with tight coupling
Synchronous RPC via broker: defeating async benefits
Broker as single point of failure: no replication/clustering
Point-to-point spaghetti: too many direct broker connections
Unbalanced broker load: hotspot from uneven partitioning
Message explosion: excessive message types without schema governance
Big broker monolith: overloading single broker instance
design_principles: Location Transparency: Clients reference services by name, not IP address or port
Loose Coupling: Producers and consumers operate independently without direct knowledge
Protocol Abstraction: Broker handles protocol translation between heterogeneous systems
Message Durability: Messages persist until successfully processed to ensure reliability
Idempotency: Consumers must handle duplicate messages safely (at-least-once delivery)
Schema Governance: Use Avro/Protobuf schemas for message contract evolution
Observability: Correlation IDs and distributed tracing enable debugging across broker hops
Failure Isolation: Circuit breakers prevent cascading failures from slow consumers
